Date of pronouncement 20.12.2025 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.1/22 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:37 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui JUDGMENT 1. By way of the present judgment, this Court proceeds to adjudicate and dispose of the complaint instituted by Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust represented by its AR Sh. Sulagno Basu (hereinafter referred to as "the complainant") against Sh. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui (hereinafter referred to as "the accused"), alleging commission of the offence punishable under Section 138 read with Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act "). The proceedings originate from the alleged dishonour of a cheque bearing no. 000042 dated 07.11.2015, drawn by the accused on his account at Kotak Mahindra Bank, Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi, for an amount of ₹1,80,000/-, purportedly issued as security against indemnification of cost incurred or to be incurred by his employer. The complainant asserts that the cheque in question was returned unpaid upon presentation to the bank due to 'Funds Insufficient'. The subsequent failure of the accused to make payment within the statutory period after service of legal demand notice has given rise to the present cause of action, leading to prosecution under the NI Act . 2. It has been categorically averred by the complainant that accused signed an appointment letter and undertaking on May 16, 2015, committing to a 36-month service period and all employment conditions, including termination procedures. Early voluntary exit required paying Rs. 1,80,000 as indemnity for recruitment, training, and related costs. A post-dated cheque bearing No. 000042 for Rs. 1,80,000/- from Kotak Mahindra Bank, Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi, secured this obligation. 3. It has been averred that the accused left the services of Moolchand Medicity on 14.10.2015 without following the due proceedure in breach of the terms of the employment. It is further averred that the accused was required to serve a notice period of 60 days before leaving his employment, however the accused left the services without proper notice. It is also alleged by the complainant that the Digitally signed by Page no.2/22 SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:40 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui accused while resigning from the post did not hand over all goods, articles, files etc and took away the same with himself. 4. That the complainant was constrained to present the post dated cheque in question that had been issued by the accused in discharge of his obligation and in terms of the settlement arrived at between the complainant and the accused. That when the complainant presented the above said cheque to its banker, the cheque got dishonoured with the remarks "funds insufficient". The said dishonour gave rise to the present cause of action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 5. Subsequent to the dishonour of the cheque, and in adherence to the statutory requirements enshrined under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant, through its engaged counsel, caused to be issued a legal demand notice dated 16.01.2016, which was dispatched to the accused via speed post. Through the said notice, the accused was unequivocally called upon to pay the dishonoured cheque amount of ₹1,80,000/- within the prescribed statutory period of fifteen days from the date of receipt. The legal notice was addressed to the residential address of the accused, as furnished by him and reiterated in the body of the complaint. 6. As per the postal records placed on record, the notice was duly dispatched to the accused on 18.01.2016. However, despite the service of the legal notice and the lapse of the mandatory statutory period, the accused neither made the payment of the cheque amount nor issued any written reply or response controverting the liability. The deliberate failure of the accused to comply with the legal demand notice, even after the dishonour of the cheque, prompted the complainant to invoke the penal provisions of the NI Act . Accordingly, the complainant instituted the present complaint under Sections 138 and 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, seeking penal consequences against the accused for wilful default and Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.3/22 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:42 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui for the enforcement of the statutory presumption of liability arising from the dishonoured negotiable instrument. 7. The complainant has categorically asserted that the conduct of the accused, in issuing a cheque that was returned unpaid on the ground of "Funds Insufficient," squarely attracts the penal provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It is further alleged that the act of the accused reflects a deliberate failure to honour his financial commitment despite due notice, thereby constituting a clear breach of the statutory mandate envisaged under the Act. 8. This deliberate act of default, when viewed in conjunction with the dishonour of the cheque on the ground of insufficiency of funds, made the complainant believe that the accused never possessed a bona fide intention to honour his financial commitments. The complainant has asserted that the sequence of events -- from the issuance of the cheque to its eventual dishonour -- unmistakably reveals a conscious and wilful breach of a legally enforceable obligation by the accused. Such conduct, as per the complainant, is not a mere instance of inadvertence or financial mismanagement but a deliberate evasion of liability, thereby squarely attracting the penal provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 9. Upon a careful perusal of the material placed on record along with the complaint, and after due examination of the complainant by way of pre-summoning evidence in accordance with the mandate of Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this Court was satisfied that a prima facie case was made out against the accused for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The evidence adduced at the pre-summoning stage sufficiently disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable liability and the issuance of the cheque in question by the accused towards its discharge, followed by its dishonour due to insufficiency of funds. Accordingly, vide order dated 04.06.2016, this Court was pleased to take cognizance of the offence andsigned Digitally by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.4/22 SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.24 16:45:44 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui summoned the accused to face trial for the alleged dishonour of cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability, as contemplated under the statutory scheme of the NI Act . 10. The accused appeared on 21.05.2018 with his counsel, and was granted bail by this Court on the very same date. Pursuant to the grant of bail, the accused was directed to furnish requisite bail bonds, and accordingly, he had furnished his bail bonds which were accepted. Subsequently, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case existed warranting trial, this Court proceeded to frame notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( CrPC ), which was duly served upon the accused on 26.07.2019. Upon being apprised of the substance of accusation, including the specific allegations pertaining to issuance and dishonour of the cheque in question, the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial, thereby necessitating the recording of evidence in the matter in accordance with law. 11. Thereafter, in support of its case, the complainant adopted its pre-summoning evidence which had been tendered earlier before the Court on 20.02.2016. Further more, the complainant examined itself through its AR Sh. Sulagno Basu who entered the witness box as CW-1. The same was followed by extensive examination, cross-examination of CW-1 on 04.05.2022 conducted on behalf of the accused and he was discharged on the same day. 13. Upon completion of the complainant evidence, same was closed on 04.05.2022 as the complainant did not wish to examine any other witnesses. 14. Hence the matter fixed for recording of statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and subsequent to the conclusion of the complainant's evidence, and in compliance with the procedural mandate under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the statement of the accused was recorded by the Court on 16.08.2022, thereby affording him an opportunity to personally explain the incriminating circumstances appearing against him in the prosecution evidence. 15. Thereafter, the accused was given a chance to lead his defense, wherein he entered the witness box as DW-1 and produced a document Ex.DW-1/1(his salary statement) in his defense. DW-1 was thoroughly cross examined by the Ld. Counsel for complainant. After the the accused was cross examined, he did not bring further evidence in his support and vide order dated 23.01.2024, DE was closed and the matter was proceeded with final arguments. Final Arguments 16. Thereafter, this Court heard the final arguments advanced on behalf of the accused on 11.11.2025. The complainant was duly afforded adequate and repeated opportunities to advance oral final arguments in support of his case. However, Page no.6/22 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:49 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui despite the grant of several adjournments, no arguments were addressed on his behalf. Consequently, the right of the complainant to address oral arguments was closed by the Court. Nonetheless, it was noted that the written arguments of both the parties are already on record. 17. The complainant submits that the present complaint under Sections 138 and 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 has been duly proved on facts and law. It is contended that the accused was appointed as Deputy Manager (Sales) with the complainant trust vide appointment letter dated 16.05.2015 and had executed an undertaking on the same date, whereby he agreed that in the event of leaving the services before completion of 36 months, he would be liable to pay a sum of Rs.1,80,000/-, being equivalent to three months' salary of Rs.60,000/- each, towards recruitment and allied costs incurred by the complainant. The cost sheet filed on record reflects the expenses incurred by the complainant in recruitment of employees. The accused admittedly left the services on 14.10.2015, in violation of the said undertaking, and in discharge of the said liability issued post-dated cheque bearing no. 000042 for Rs.1,80,000/-. 18. The cheque, upon presentation, was dishonoured for "insufficient funds" vide return memo dated 19.12.2015. Thereafter, statutory legal demand notice dated 16.01.2016 was duly issued and served upon the accused, but despite receipt, the accused failed to make payment within the prescribed period, compelling the complainant to institute the present complaint within limitation. 19. It is further argued that the complainant, being a Trust running Moolchand Hospital, is competent to maintain the present complaint, and reliance is placed on precedents to submit that a trust can sue and be sued and is covered within the framework of the Negotiable Instruments Act . 20. The complainant submits that the accused has unequivocally admitted his signatures on the cheque as well as on the appointment letter and undertaking, including in his statement under Section 313 CrPC and during cross-examination. Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.7/22 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:51 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui Once the signatures are admitted, the statutory presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act arise in favour of the complainant that the cheque was issued for consideration and in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. 21. Reliance is placed upon the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Triyambak S. Hegde v. Sripad , K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan , Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat , Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee and Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh to contend that the burden lies on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption by raising a probable defence, which cannot be discharged by mere denial. 22. It is argued that the accused has failed to rebut the presumption as he has neither put any meaningful challenge to the complainant's witness regarding the undertaking and liability, nor raised any such defence at the stage of framing of notice, statement under Section 313 CrPC, or by leading cogent defence evidence. The bank statement relied upon by the accused, showing deductions from salary, is stated to be on account of TDS, leave deductions and PF, and does not negate the contractual liability under the undertaking. 23. The complainant further submits that all the essential ingredients of Section 138 of the Act, as summarized by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gimpex (P) Ltd. v. Manoj Goel , stand satisfied in the present case, namely: drawing of the cheque by the accused on his account, issuance in discharge of a legally enforceable liability, presentation within validity, dishonour due to insufficiency of funds, issuance and service of statutory notice within time, and failure of the accused to make payment within 15 days. On these premises, the complainant prays that the accused be convicted for the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and be directed to pay compensation equal to the cheque amount along with interest, as deemed fit by the Court. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.8/22 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:52 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui 24. The accused submits that the present complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not maintainable and deserves dismissal on facts as well as in law. 25. It is contended that the complainant Trust runs Moolchand Medcity Hospital and that the present complaint has been filed through an authorised representative. However, during cross-examination, the AR failed to produce the original board resolution and admitted that he joined the complainant only in the year 2021, whereas the accused had left service in 2015. It is argued that the AR had no personal knowledge of the transaction in question, thereby rendering his testimony unreliable. 26. The accused submits that the impugned cheque bearing no. 000042 for Rs. 1,80,000/- was not issued towards any legally enforceable debt or liability but was given merely as a security cheque at the time of employment. It is further argued that even as per the documents relied upon by the complainant, the cheque was blank, and hence its misuse vitiates the complaint. 27. It is further contended that since the complainant is a Trust, the complaint could have been instituted only through a duly executed power of attorney by the trustees. The present complaint having been filed merely on the basis of an alleged authorisation/resolution is stated to be defective, and therefore not maintainable. 28. On merits, it is argued that the accused was compelled to leave the services of the complainant on 14.10.2015 as he was not paid his full salary in terms of the appointment letter. It is submitted that no recruitment cost was in fact incurred by the complainant, no training was imparted, and no gadgets or facilities were provided to the accused. Hence, the claim of Rs. 1,80,000/- towards alleged recruitment cost is stated to be false and without basis. 29. The accused further contends that the clause requiring payment of such amount on leaving service amounts to an unreasonable restraint of trade and is unenforceable. Page no.9/22 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:54 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui In the absence of any legally enforceable liability, the essential ingredient of Section 138 of the NI Act is not satisfied. On these grounds, the accused prays that the complaint be dismissed and he be acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Legal Analysis & Findings:- 30. I have heard at considerable length the detailed arguments advanced by the learned counsel appearing for the complainant as well as the learned counsel representing the accused. Their respective submissions have been carefully analysed in the context of the factual matrix and the legal principles applicable to the case. This Court has also undertaken a thorough and meticulous scrutiny of the entire judicial record, which includes the contents of the complaint, the affidavits and supporting documents annexed thereto, the oral testimonies of the complainant's and the defence witnesses recorded during the course of trial, and all exhibits relied upon by the respective parties. Each piece of evidence has been examined individually as well as in conjunction with the other evidence on record so as to assess its evidentiary value, credibility, and probative strength. The rival submissions have been objectively evaluated against the backdrop of the statutory framework and the well-settled legal position governing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Court has, therefore, endeavoured to reach a reasoned and just determination by adopting a holistic and balanced appreciation of the evidence and circumstances presented before it. 31. Before embarking upon a discussion on the merits of the present case, it is considered apposite to first delineate the legal framework governing the offence of dishonour of cheque, as encapsulated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The legislative intent behind enacting Section 138 is to instill greater financial discipline and sanctity in contractual obligations by deterring the issuance of cheques without sufficient funds or without adequate arrangements with the banker. The provision prescribes penal consequences in the Digitally signed Page no.10/22 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:45:56 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui event of dishonor of a cheque on grounds of insufficiency of funds or if the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank, thereby recognizing the cheque as a legitimate instrument of payment in the eyes of the law. 32. In order to fasten criminal liability upon an accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it is incumbent upon the complainant to plead and prove the existence of certain foundational ingredients through the averments made in the complaint and the evidence led during the course of trial. The essential ingredients that must be cumulatively satisfied are as follows: a. That the accused must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker, for the payment of a certain sum of money to another person, and such payment must have been intended for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability; b. That the said cheque must have been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn, or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; c. That upon such presentation, the cheque must have been returned unpaid by the bank, either due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement made by the drawer with the bank; d. That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must have issued a written statutory demand notice to the drawer, seeking payment of the cheque amount, within 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid; e. That the drawer of the cheque, despite the receipt of such legal notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or holder in due course within 15 days from the date of such receipt. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.11/22 SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.24 16:45:58 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui 33. Only upon proof of the aforementioned ingredients does the offence under Section 138 stand attracted, subject to the operation of statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. These presumptions, however, are rebuttable and impose a reverse burden upon the accused to dislodge the same on a preponderance of probabilities. 34. It is also pertinent to note that, as per the Explanation appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the expression "debt or other liability" refers exclusively to a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This legal clarification is of critical significance, as it makes clear that mere issuance of a cheque is not sufficient to attract penal liability under the statute. The dishonoured cheque must have been issued in discharge of a debt or liability which is subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance. A cheque issued as a gift, donation, or towards a time-barred or non-existent liability will not fall within the purview of Section 138 . Thus, the complainant must establish that at the time the cheque was drawn, there existed a valid and enforceable obligation in law for which the cheque was issued. 35. It is well-settled in law that the aforementioned ingredients must co-exist and be satisfied cumulatively in order to constitute the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The absence or non-fulfilment of even one of these statutory requirements is fatal to the prosecution's case and would disentitle the complainant from invoking penal liability against the drawer of the cheque. 36. CW-1, Sh. Sulagno Basu, deposed that he is working as Senior Manager - Corporate Affairs with the complainant hospital and has been duly authorised vide trust resolution dated 29.05.2019 (Ex. CW1/1) to depose and institute proceedings on behalf of the complainant trust, which runs Moolchand Medcity Hospital at Lajpat Nagar-III, New Delhi. He stated that the accused, Shadab Anwar Siddiqui, was employed as Deputy Manager (Sales) with effect from Page no.12/22 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:00 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui 16.05.2015. As per the appointment letter and undertaking dated 16.05.2015 (Ex. CW1/2 and Ex. CW1/3), the accused had agreed to serve for a minimum period of 36 months and, in case of leaving service earlier on his own, to pay Rs. 1,80,000/- towards indemnification of costs incurred or to be incurred by the hospital for selection, training, induction, etc. In support of this undertaking, the accused issued a post-dated cheque bearing no. 000042 dated for Rs. 1,80,000/- drawn on Kotak Mahindra Bank, Lajpat Nagar, New Delhi, in favour of Moolchand Medcity, which is exhibited as Ex. CW1/4. 37. CW-1 further deposed that the accused left the services of the complainant on 14.10.2015 in breach of the terms of employment, without serving the stipulated notice period of 60 days and without proper handover of articles and responsibilities. He stated that the undertaking constituted a valid contract and that upon such premature exit, the amount of Rs. 1,80,000/- became a legally recoverable liability of the accused. He testified that the cheque was presented by the complainant but was returned unpaid with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide return memo dated 19.12.2015, exhibited as Ex. CW1/5. 38. CW-1 further stated that the complainant incurs substantial expenditure towards recruitment and training of employees, including costs of HR resources, job portals, interviews, induction and training, and that such costs are apportioned per employee. The cost sheet reflecting such expenses was exhibited as Ex. CW1/6. He deposed that thereafter a statutory demand notice dated 16.01.2016 was issued to the accused calling upon him to pay the cheque amount within 15 days. The said notice was duly served on 19.01.2016. The legal notice, postal receipts and proof of delivery are exhibited as Ex. CW1/7, Ex. CW1/8 and Ex. CW1/9 respectively. Despite service, the accused neither paid the cheque amount nor sent any reply. 39. CW-1 concluded by stating that the accused has failed to discharge his legally enforceable liability of Rs. 1,80,000/- and has thereby committed the offence Page no.13/22 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:02 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and prayed that the accused be punished and the complainant be duly compensated. 40. In cross-examination, CW-1 stated that he joined the complainant hospital in 2008 as a Management Trainee and was promoted over time, lastly as Senior Manager in April 2021. He admitted that the resolution Ex. CW1/1 authorising him is generic in nature and not case-specific. He deposed that he was posted as Manager (Operations) in 2015 and was senior to the accused, though in a different department. 41. CW-1 admitted that he was not fully aware of all the contents of the accused's appointment letter and that the appointment letter does not contain any clause requiring payment of Rs. 1,80,000/-. He further admitted that as per clause 6 of Ex. CW1/2, an amount of Rs. 60,000/- was to be retained as security by the complainant. However, he denied that the cheque in question was a security cheque and volunteered that it was an indemnity cheque issued pursuant to the undertaking. He confirmed that the cheque in question is the same cheque referred to in the undertaking Ex. CW1/3. 42. He denied the suggestion that the complainant had filled in the date on the cheque and stated that the cheque was issued in favour of Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services. He asserted that Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services is run by the complainant trust and that the bank account is maintained in that name, though he admitted that he did not have any document at that time to show that the said entity is part of the trust. 43. CW-1 denied the suggestion that the complainant is not the payee or is not authorised to file the present complaint, and also denied that there was no legally recoverable debt or that the cheque was misused. He further denied that there was any discrepancy between the undertaking and the cheque or that he was deposing falsely or without personal knowledge, asserting that he was aware of the transaction. Thereafter, CW-1 stated that he is the authorised representative of the complainant trust and that the complainant does not wish to examine any further witness, and accordingly closed the complainant's evidence. 45. He asserted that Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services is run by the complainant trust and that the bank account is maintained in that name, though he admitted that he did not have any document at that time to show that the said entity is part of the trust. 48. He further denied that there was any discrepancy between the undertaking and the cheque or that he was deposing Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.15/22 SHARMA SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.24 16:46:06 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui falsely or without personal knowledge, asserting that he was aware of the transaction. 49. Thereafter, CW-1 stated that he is the authorised representative of the complainant trust and that the complainant does not wish to examine any further witness, and accordingly closed the complainant's evidence 50. At the very outset, it is apposite to reiterate the settled legal position that in a prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant is not only required to establish the foundational facts pertaining to the issuance of the cheque, its presentation within the period of validity, its dishonour for a legally recognised reason, and the issuance and service of the statutory demand notice followed by non-payment within the prescribed period, but must also demonstrate its locus standi to institute and prosecute the complaint. This requirement assumes particular significance where the complainant is not a natural person but a juristic entity such as a company or a firm, which can act only through its authorised human agency. In such cases, the complainant must place on record cogent material to show that the person who has instituted the complaint, signed the pleadings, and entered the witness box is duly authorised, either by a valid board resolution, power of attorney, or any other legally recognised mode of delegation, to represent the juristic entity in legal proceedings. 51. The rationale underlying this requirement is that while a company or corporation has a distinct legal personality in the eyes of law, it lacks physical existence and can neither depose nor act on its own; therefore, its acts before a court must necessarily be carried out through an authorised representative who is competent to depose on its behalf. The law thus insists that such authorisation must be explicit and demonstrable from the record, so as to ensure that the prosecution is not launched by an unauthorised person and that the entity in whose name the complaint is filed is in fact the real aggrieved party. Digitally signed by Page no.16/22 SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:09 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui 52. It is equally well settled that once such authorisation is duly proved, the authorised representative is competent not only to institute the complaint but also to depose as a witness on behalf of the complainant, provided his testimony is based either on personal knowledge of the transaction or on perusal of the records maintained by the complainant in the ordinary course of business. The authorised representative, in such a situation, steps into the shoes of the complainant for the purposes of the proceedings, and his acts and testimony bind the juristic entity. 53. Therefore, in a complaint under Section 138 NI Act instituted by a company or other juristic person, proof of proper authorisation and locus standi is not a mere procedural formality but a foundational requirement going to the very maintainability of the complaint. Unless the complainant discharges this initial burden, the prosecution itself would be rendered vulnerable. It is in this legal backdrop that the locus standi and authority of the complainant's representative in the present case are required to be examined. 54. In the present case, the complaint has been instituted in the name of Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust through its purported authorised representative, CW-1 Sh. Sulagno Basu. In order to establish his locus standi, CW-1 has relied upon a copy of an alleged resolution dated 29.05.2019, exhibited as Ex. CW1/1, to contend that he was authorised to institute and prosecute the present complaint on behalf of the complainant trust. 55. However, a careful scrutiny of the evidence reveals serious infirmities in the proof of such authorisation. During his cross-examination, CW-1 has candidly admitted that: (i) the original resolution was never produced before the Court; (ii) the said resolution is generic in nature and does not specifically authorise him to institute or prosecute the present complaint against the accused; and (iii) he joined the complainant trust in a managerial capacity much after the year 2015 and had no direct involvement in or personal knowledge of the transaction in question, which forms the substratum of the present case. It is pertinent to note that the accused had specifically objected to the mode of proof of Ex. CW1/1 at the time of its exhibition. Despite such objection, the complainant failed to cure the defect by producing the original resolution or by leading secondary evidence in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act . More importantly, no trustee, office bearer, or any other competent person connected with the management of the trust was examined to prove that any such resolution was in fact passed and that CW-1 was duly authorised thereunder to represent the trust before this Court. The document Ex. CW1/1, therefore, remains an unproved and inadmissible piece of evidence. 57. It is trite law that when a complaint is filed on behalf of a juristic entity, be it a company, trust, or society, the person representing such entity must affirmatively establish, by cogent evidence, that he is duly authorised to institute and prosecute the proceedings. Such authorisation cannot be presumed and must be specifically pleaded and proved. In this regard, reliance may be placed on the authoritative pronouncement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra , (2014) 11 SCC 790, wherein it has been categorically held that the power to file a complaint under Section 138 NI Act and to depose on behalf of the complainant must flow from a specific authorisation, duly proved in accordance with law. 58. In the present case, the failure of the complainant to produce and prove the original resolution or any valid authorisation goes to the very root of the matter. In the absence of proof that CW-1 was duly empowered by the complainant trust to institute and prosecute the present complaint, his locus standi remains unestablished. Consequently, CW-1 cannot be treated as a duly authorised representative of the complainant, and the very institution of the complaint is rendered doubtful and legally unsustainable. On this ground alone, the complaint is liable to fail as not maintainable. Another serious and fundamental infirmity in the complainant's case lies in its failure to establish the identity of the payee named on the cheque and its nexus with the complainant trust. 60. As per the complainant's own pleadings and evidence, the cheque in question has been drawn in favour of "Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services", whereas the complaint before this Court has been instituted by "Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust". Thus, on the face of the record itself, the payee named on the cheque and the complainant before the Court are not the same entities. 61. During cross-examination, CW-1 has categorically admitted that he does not possess any document to show that "Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services" is a unit, department, constituent arm, or trade name of the complainant trust. Though he volunteered that he could produce such a document, no such document was ever brought on record during the entire course of trial. This omission assumes significance, particularly when the very maintainability of the complaint depends upon the complainant establishing that it is either the payee or a holder in due course of the cheque. 62. The ambiguity is further compounded by clause 6 of the undertaking Ex. CW1/3, which refers to issuance of cheque in favour of "Moolchand Khairati Ram Hospital", whereas the cheque itself stands in the name of "Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services". The complainant has neither explained this discrepancy nor led any evidence to show that these expressions refer to the same legal entity or are merely different descriptions of the complainant trust. Such inconsistencies strike at the root of the complainant's case. 63. In the absence of any documentary material such as the trust deed, certificate of registration, bank mandate, account opening form, correspondence with the bank, or any other contemporaneous record to demonstrate that: (i) "Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services" is in fact the same entity as, or a unit of, Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust; or Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.19/22 SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:16 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui (ii) that the complainant trust is legally authorised or entitled to receive payment on behalf of the said payee, this Court is left with no basis to presume any nexus between the two. 64. It is well settled that under Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a complaint under Section 138 can be instituted only by the "payee" or the "holder in due course" of the cheque. The burden squarely lies on the complainant to establish that it answers either of these descriptions. In the present case, the complainant has failed to discharge this burden. There is no evidence on record to show that the complainant trust is the payee named in the cheque or that it has derived title to the cheque as a holder in due course. 65. The failure to establish this crucial link is not a mere technical defect but goes to the very root of the matter. In the absence of proof that the complainant is legally entitled to maintain the present complaint with respect to the cheque drawn in favour of a differently named entity, the maintainability of the complaint itself becomes gravely doubtful. Consequently, the complainant's case suffers from a fatal defect on this score as well. 66. Though the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, such admission by itself does not automatically entitle the complainant to the benefit of the statutory presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It is trite that these presumptions arise only when the complainant first establishes the foundational facts, namely, that the cheque was drawn in favour of the complainant and that the complainant is legally competent to enforce the instrument as the payee or as a holder in due course. The presumption of consideration and of legally enforceable debt is not an abstract presumption in vacuum, but one that operates in favour of a complainant who demonstrates locus standi in terms of Section 142 of the NI Act. 67. Where the very status of the complainant as the payee or holder in due course is in doubt, or where the complainant fails to prove that it is the entity in whose favour the cheque has been issued, the statutory presumptions cannot be invoked. In Page no.20/22 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:19 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui other words, unless the complainant shows that it is legally entitled to receive the cheque amount and to maintain the prosecution, the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 do not come into play, notwithstanding admission of signatures by the accused. 68. In the present case, as discussed hereinabove, the complainant has failed to establish two fundamental aspects: (i) that CW-1 was duly and validly authorised to institute and prosecute the present complaint on behalf of the complainant trust; and (ii) that the complainant trust bears any legal identity or nexus with the payee named on the cheque, namely "Moolchand Hospital Allopathy Services", so as to qualify as the payee or holder in due course. 69. In the absence of proof of due authorisation and in the absence of any documentary evidence demonstrating that the complainant is the same entity as, or is legally entitled to act for and receive payment on behalf of, the named payee, the very locus standi of the complainant remains unestablished. These defects go to the root of the matter. 70. Consequently, this Court holds that the foundational facts necessary to trigger the statutory presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act remain unproved in the present case. The complainant, therefore, cannot seek aid of the said presumptions merely on the strength of the accused's admission of signatures on the cheque, when its own entitlement to enforce the cheque has not been established in accordance with law. 71. The defects noticed hereinabove are not mere technical irregularities or curable lapses, but go to the very root of the matter, striking at the competence and locus standi of the complainant to institute and maintain the present proceedings. In a criminal prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant is required, at the threshold, to establish its entitlement to maintain the complaint and the authority of the person who represents it before the Court. Failure to do so renders the very institution of the complaint suspect. Page no.21/22 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.24 16:46:22 +0530 Ct case no. 620669/2016 Shri Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust vs. Shadab Anwar Siddiqui 72. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of every reasonable doubt, and that the burden to prove the maintainability of the complaint and the complainant's locus standi lies squarely upon the complainant. Such burden cannot be shifted upon the accused, nor can it be presumed in the absence of cogent proof. In the present case, despite specific objection by the defence, the complainant has failed to discharge this foundational burden. 73. Accordingly, this Court is of the considered opinion that the complainant has failed to establish that the present complaint has been instituted through a duly authorised person and further failed to prove that the complainant Trust is the payee or holder in due course, or otherwise legally entitled to enforce the cheque in question. This infirmity strikes at the very maintainability of the complaint and vitiates the prosecution at its inception. Conclusion 74. In the light of the aforementioned discussion, the accused is therefore acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 75.
